1. Introduction & Approach

Tintinalli Ch.176 p.1187
  • Poisoning is among the leading causes of injury-related death; over 2.4 million human exposures reported annually to US Poison Control Centers.
  • Clinical priorities: (1) ABCs + rapid resuscitation; (2) recognize the toxidrome; (3) decontamination if appropriate; (4) administer antidotes when available; (5) enhanced elimination if indicated; (6) supportive care.
  • "Treat the patient, not the poison" — supportive care and meticulous monitoring save more lives than any antidote.
  • Always consider polypharmacy — most intentional ingestions involve multiple substances.
  • Poison Control Center: 1-800-222-1222 (US) — invaluable resource for guidance.

2. Initial Resuscitation

Tintinalli p.1187–1188

Standard ABCDE approach with toxicology modifications

  • Airway: protect early in obtunded patients; consider RSI agents that don't worsen toxicity.
  • Breathing: avoid disrupting compensatory hyperventilation (e.g., salicylate); match minute ventilation if intubated.
  • Circulation: aggressive volume resuscitation; specific antidotes for cardiotoxic poisons.
  • Disability: glucose, naloxone, thiamine in altered mental status (the "coma cocktail").
  • Exposure: full undressing for skin decontamination; check for transdermal patches.

The "coma cocktail" — empirical drugs for AMS of unknown cause

  • Dextrose 50% 25 g IV (or fingerstick first; 0.5–1 g/kg in pediatric).
  • Naloxone 0.04–2 mg IV/IM/IN — titrate; lower dose if chronic opioid use to avoid precipitated withdrawal.
  • Thiamine 100 mg IV — before glucose in suspected alcoholism (prevent Wernicke's).
  • Flumazenil — NOT routinely recommended; risk of seizure in mixed overdoses (TCA, etc.).
Pearl — empirical "coma cocktail": always check glucose first (cheap, immediate). Naloxone for suspected opioid toxicity. Thiamine before glucose in suspected alcoholism. Avoid flumazenil unless single-agent benzodiazepine overdose with respiratory failure.

3. Toxin-Induced Cardiac Arrest

Tintinalli Table 176-1 p.1188
📚 Table 176-1 — Potential Interventions in Toxin-Induced Cardiac Arrest (Tintinalli p.1188)

Toxin-specific interventions

Toxin / MechanismSpecific intervention
DigoxinDigoxin Fab fragments
Organophosphates / carbamatesAtropine + pralidoxime
Envenomation (snake, etc.)Specific antivenom
Sodium channel blocker / wide-QRS tachycardia (TCA, cocaine, etc.)Sodium bicarbonate
Calcium channel blocker / β-blockerHigh-dose insulin (HDI) infusion
Local anesthetic toxicity / lipophilic cardiotoxinsIV lipid emulsion (Intralipid 20%)

Other adjuncts when standard ACLS fails

  • Cardiac pacing for refractory bradycardia
  • Intra-aortic balloon pump
  • VA-ECMO / extracorporeal life support — rescue therapy for refractory cardiogenic shock
⚠️ Pearl — toxicologic cardiac arrest: Standard ACLS may fail. Consider toxin-specific therapy early. VA-ECMO is increasingly used as a bridge in toxic cardiogenic shock — discuss with poison control + cardiology early.

Inline MCQ 1. Which is the antidote for cyanide poisoning preferred for fire smoke inhalation victims?

Answer: B. Hydroxocobalamin is preferred for smoke inhalation cyanide because it doesn't worsen the methemoglobinemia of concomitant CO poisoning (vs sodium nitrite). Reference: Tintinalli Table 176-2.

5. Agitation, Hyperthermia, Hypothermia

Tintinalli p.1188

Toxin-induced agitation

  • Benzodiazepines first-line — titrated lorazepam 1–2 mg IV q5min, midazolam 2–5 mg IV/IM, diazepam 5–10 mg IV.
  • Antipsychotics (haloperidol, droperidol) often given but have theoretical disadvantages: QT prolongation, lowered seizure threshold, dystonic/extrapyramidal effects.
  • Ketamine 4 mg/kg IM for severe excited delirium refractory to benzodiazepines.
  • Phenytoin is NOT useful for toxin-induced seizures and should not be used.

Hyperthermia

  • Core temp >39°C (>102.2°F) requires aggressive cooling.
  • Common causes: anticholinergic, sympathomimetic (cocaine, MDMA), serotonin syndrome, NMS, malignant hyperthermia.
  • Active external cooling (evaporative, ice bath, cooling blankets) + sedation to reduce muscle activity.
  • Consider neuromuscular paralysis + intubation in severe rhabdomyolysis or refractory hyperthermia.
  • Antipyretics are ineffective in toxin-induced hyperthermia (not pyrogenic).

Hypothermia

  • Toxin-induced (sedative-hypnotic OD, ethanol) — manage as standard hypothermia (Ch.209).
  • Core temperature monitoring + active rewarming.

6. History & Examination

Tintinalli Table 176-3 p.1189

Key elements of the history

  • Substance(s): name, formulation (IR vs ER), amount, route, time of ingestion.
  • All medications in the household — patient's, others' (especially in pediatric ingestions).
  • Co-ingestants: alcohol, recreational drugs, OTC products.
  • Intent: intentional vs accidental; suicide risk assessment for intentional.
  • Past medical / psychiatric history.
  • Exposure circumstances: workplace, recreational, environmental.
📚 Table 176-3 — Examination of the Poisoned Patient: organ system findings + likely toxic significance (Tintinalli p.1189)

Examination clues

  • General: mental status, dress, odors (gasoline, almonds = cyanide, garlic = organophosphates), nutritional state.
  • Vital signs: bradycardia (β-blocker, CCB, digoxin, opioid), tachycardia (sympathomimetic, anticholinergic), hyperthermia, hypotension/HTN, RR.
  • Pupils: miosis (opioid, organophosphate, clonidine), mydriasis (anticholinergic, sympathomimetic), nystagmus (anticonvulsant, ETOH).
  • Skin: diaphoresis (sympathomimetic, cholinergic), dry warm flushed (anticholinergic), needle tracks (IV drug use), bullae (barbiturate prolonged coma), patches.
  • Reflexes: hyperreflexia + clonus (serotonin syndrome), hyporeflexia (sedative-hypnotic).
  • Muscle tone: rigidity (NMS, serotonin), fasciculations (cholinergic).
Pearl — Always check pockets and skin: remove all clothing for full body inspection. Look for transdermal patches, IV access devices, infusion pumps. A patient who took a "lethal dose" of pills may have a transdermal fentanyl patch contributing too.

7. Common Toxidromes (★ HIGH-YIELD)

Tintinalli Table 176-4 p.1190
📚 Table 176-4 — Common Toxidromes: Anticholinergic, Cholinergic, Opioid, Sympathomimetic, Sedative-hypnotic, Serotonin, NMS, Hallucinogen, Salicylate, Hypoglycemic, Extrapyramidal (Tintinalli p.1190)

The classic toxidromes — pattern recognition saves lives

ToxidromeExamplesHallmarks
AnticholinergicAtropine, antihistamines, TCA, antipsychotics, Datura"Mad as a hatter, blind as a bat, dry as a bone, red as a beet, hot as a hare" — AMS, mydriasis, dry skin/mucous, hyperthermia, tachycardia, urinary retention, ↓ bowel sounds
CholinergicOrganophosphates, carbamates, sarin (nerve agents)SLUDGE-M / DUMBBELS — Salivation, Lacrimation, Urination, Defecation, GI distress, Emesis + Miosis. Muscle fasciculations, weakness
OpioidHeroin, morphine, oxycodoneTriad: miosis + respiratory depression + CNS depression
SympathomimeticCocaine, amphetamines, MDMA, cathinonesHTN + tachycardia + hyperthermia + diaphoresis (NOT dry) + mydriasis + agitation
Sedative-hypnoticBenzodiazepines, barbiturates, ETOHCNS depression + dysarthria + ataxia + bradycardia + respiratory depression
Serotonin syndromeSSRIs, MAOIs, tramadol, fentanyl, MDMA, St. John's wort, linezolidAMS + hyperthermia + autonomic instability + clonus (lower > upper) + hyperreflexia + tremor
NMSAntipsychotics"Lead-pipe rigidity" + bradyreflexia + hyperthermia + AMS + autonomic instability (dopamine antagonism)
HallucinogenPCP, LSD, mescalineHallucinations + dysphoria + anxiety + N/V + sympathomimetic signs
SalicylateAspirin, oil of wintergreenAMS + respiratory alkalosis + AG metabolic acidosis + tinnitus + tachypnea + diaphoresis + hyperpyrexia
HypoglycemicInsulin, sulfonylureasAMS + diaphoresis + tachycardia + HTN + dysarthria + behavioral change + seizures
ExtrapyramidalRisperidone, haloperidol, phenothiazinesDystonia, torticollis, muscle rigidity, choreoathetosis, hyperreflexia, seizures
The big distinguishing pearl:
• Anticholinergic vs Sympathomimetic — both have HTN, tachycardia, hyperthermia, mydriasis, AMS. Distinguish by SKIN: anticholinergic = dry hot; sympathomimetic = wet diaphoretic.
• Cholinergic SLUDGE-M: Salivation, Lacrimation, Urination, Defecation, GI cramping, Emesis + Miosis.
• Cholinergic DUMBBELS: Defecation, Urination, Miosis, Bradycardia/Bronchospasm/Bronchorrhea, Emesis, Lacrimation, Salivation.
• NMS vs Serotonin syndrome: NMS = lead-pipe rigidity; Serotonin = clonus (lower extremities ≫ upper) + hyperreflexia.
Inline MCQ 2. A patient presents with HTN, tachycardia, hyperthermia, mydriasis, AMS, and dry hot skin with absent bowel sounds. Which toxidrome is this?
A. Sympathomimetic
Incorrect option. Compare against the correct choice and rationale below.
B. Anticholinergic
Correct option. Read the full rationale below.
C. Serotonin syndrome
Incorrect option. Compare against the correct choice and rationale below.
D. NMS
Incorrect option. Compare against the correct choice and rationale below.
Answer: B. "Mad as a hatter, blind as a bat, dry as a bone, red as a beet, hot as a hare" — anticholinergic. Sympathomimetic has DIAPHORESIS (wet skin). Reference: Tintinalli Table 176-4.
Inline MCQ 3. Which finding distinguishes serotonin syndrome from NMS?
A. Hyperthermia
Incorrect option. Compare against the correct choice and rationale below.
B. Altered mental status
Incorrect option. Compare against the correct choice and rationale below.
C. Clonus (especially in lower extremities) + hyperreflexia (serotonin) vs lead-pipe rigidity + bradyreflexia (NMS)
Correct option. Read the full rationale below.
D. Autonomic instability
Incorrect option. Compare against the correct choice and rationale below.
Answer: C. Both have hyperthermia + AMS + autonomic instability. Serotonin = clonus (lower > upper) + hyperreflexia + tremor. NMS = lead-pipe rigidity + bradyreflexia. Onset: serotonin within 24 h; NMS over days. Reference: Tintinalli Table 176-4.

8. Diagnostic Testing

Tintinalli Tables 176-5 & 176-6 p.1190

Routine "tox screen" pitfalls

  • Standard urine drug screens use immunoassay — high false-positive AND false-negative rates.
  • Positive does not mean intoxicated; negative does not exclude a substance.
  • Most board questions test understanding of which drugs miss standard screens.
📚 Table 176-6 — Standard Enzyme-Immunoassay Urine Drug Screens: false positives & false negatives by class (Tintinalli p.1191)

Useful serum drug levels for management

📚 Table 176-5 — Drug Serum Measurements That May Assist Patient Assessment or Management (Tintinalli p.1190)

Drugs with measurable, clinically useful serum levels

  • Acetaminophen (Rumack-Matthew nomogram)
  • Salicylate (severity grading + HD criteria)
  • Carbamazepine, phenobarbital, phenytoin, valproic acid
  • Digoxin (consider Fab if >10 ng/mL acute or >6 chronic)
  • Ethanol, methanol, ethylene glycol
  • Iron, lithium
  • Carbon monoxide (carboxyhemoglobin)
  • Methemoglobin
  • Theophylline
  • Paraquat

Common false positives on UDS (mnemonic: "BPMRSTL")

  • Amphetamine immunoassay false-positives: bupropion, pseudoephedrine, ranitidine, trazodone, phenethylamine
  • Methadone immunoassay false-positives: doxylamine, diphenhydramine, quetiapine
  • Phencyclidine immunoassay false-positives: diphenhydramine, dextromethorphan, ketamine, tramadol, venlafaxine
  • Tricyclic immunoassay false-positives: carbamazepine, cyclobenzaprine, diphenhydramine, quetiapine, hydroxyzine

Common false negatives

  • Synthetic cathinones ("bath salts") — miss standard amphetamine screens
  • Synthetic cannabinoids ("K2/spice") — miss THC screens
  • Designer fentanyl analogues — may miss standard opioid screens
  • Newer benzodiazepines (lorazepam, clonazepam) — may miss; oxazepam-based assays may not detect
  • Oxycodone, hydrocodone — may miss "opiate" screens (target morphine/codeine); need specific assay

Incorrect option. Compare against the correct choice and rationale below.

C. Diphenhydramine, carbamazepine, cyclobenzaprine, quetiapine

D. Naproxen
Incorrect option. Compare against the correct choice and rationale below.
Answer: C. Diphenhydramine, carbamazepine, cyclobenzaprine, quetiapine, hydroxyzine all cross-react. Reference: Tintinalli Table 176-6.

9. GI Decontamination

Tintinalli Tables 176-7, 176-8 p.1192
📚 Table 176-7 — Indications, Contraindications, and Complications of GI Decontamination Procedures (Tintinalli p.1192)

Modalities (rarely used; case-by-case)

  • Activated charcoal (single dose, 1 g/kg): within 1–2 h of ingestion of carbon-adsorbable substance + airway protected. Most useful procedure.
  • Orogastric lavage: within 1 h of life-threatening ingestion + airway protected. Rarely indicated; primarily large pill ingestion or massive overdose where AC won't suffice.
  • Whole-bowel irrigation (PEG): ingested objects not adsorbed by AC (iron, lithium, lead, sustained-release products), packers/stuffers, body packers.
  • Activated charcoal multidose: drugs with enterohepatic circulation (carbamazepine, phenobarbital, dapsone, theophylline, quinine).
  • Cathartics (sorbitol): not recommended routinely; risk dehydration.
📚 Table 176-8 — Principles to Minimize Complications From Orogastric Lavage (Tintinalli p.1192)

What does NOT bind to activated charcoal

  • "PHAILS" mnemonic:
    • Pesticides
    • Hydrocarbons (caustics — and risk aspiration)
    • Acids / Alkali (caustics)
    • Iron
    • Lithium
    • Solvents / Salts (potassium, sodium)
  • Also: alcohols, fluoride, heavy metals (Pb, Hg, As).
Pearl — when AC is contraindicated: caustic ingestion (no benefit, worsens endoscopy view), unprotected airway with risk of aspiration, gastric perforation, ileus, and substances on the PHAILS list. Consider WBI for iron, lithium, lead, body packers.

B. Salicylate
Incorrect option. Compare against the correct choice and rationale below.
C. Tricyclic antidepressant
Incorrect option. Compare against the correct choice and rationale below.
D. Iron
Correct option. Read the full rationale below.
Answer: D. PHAILS list — Pesticides, Hydrocarbons, Acids/Alkali, Iron, Lithium, Solvents/Salts. Iron requires WBI. Reference: Tintinalli p.1192.

10. Enhanced Elimination

Tintinalli Tables 176-9, 176-10, 176-11 p.1193
📚 Table 176-9 — Enhanced Elimination Procedures: indications, contraindications, complications (Tintinalli p.1193)

Multidose activated charcoal

  • Indications: drugs with enterohepatic circulation — carbamazepine, dapsone, phenobarbital, quinine, theophylline ("memorize CDPST").
  • Loading: 1 g/kg PO, then 0.5 g/kg q2–4h × 3 doses.
  • Contraindications: ileus, intestinal obstruction, perforation, unprotected airway.

Urinary alkalinization

📚 Table 176-10 — Protocol for Urinary Alkalinization in Adults with Normal Renal Function (Tintinalli p.1193)
  • Indications: moderate–severe salicylate toxicity (not meeting HD criteria); phenobarbital; chlorophenoxy herbicides (2,4-D, MCPA, mecoprop).
  • Protocol: NaHCO₃ 1–2 mEq/kg bolus → infusion 150 mEq in 1 L D5W at 1.5–2× maintenance. Target serum pH 7.50–7.55, urine pH ≥7.5.
  • Add KCl 20–40 mEq/L — hypokalemia prevents urine alkalinization.

Extracorporeal removal (HD, hemoperfusion, CRRT)

📚 Table 176-11 — Extracorporeal Removal Techniques: indications, contraindications, complications (Tintinalli p.1193)

Drugs amenable to hemodialysis

  • Toxin properties favoring HD: low Vd (<1 L/kg), low protein binding, low molecular weight, high water solubility.
  • Classic dialyzable drugs: lithium, salicylate, methanol, ethylene glycol, theophylline, valproic acid, metformin (severe lactic acidosis), barbiturates (long-acting).
  • Mnemonic "I STUMBLED": Isopropanol (rare), Salicylates, Theophylline, Uremia, Methanol/Methotrexate, Barbiturates, Lithium, Ethylene glycol, Dabigatran (rare).
Hemoperfusion vs HD:
• Hemodialysis: for water-soluble + low-protein-bound + low-MW drugs.
• Hemoperfusion: for highly protein-bound + lipid-soluble drugs (was used for theophylline, paraquat — but high-flux HD is now often as effective).
Inline MCQ 6. Which substance is BEST removed by hemodialysis?
A. Tricyclic antidepressant (large Vd)
Incorrect option. Compare against the correct choice and rationale below.
B. Digoxin (large Vd, high protein binding)
Incorrect option. Compare against the correct choice and rationale below.
C. Lithium (low Vd, no protein binding)
Correct option. Read the full rationale below.
D. Iron
Incorrect option. Compare against the correct choice and rationale below.
Answer: C. Lithium has small Vd (~0.7 L/kg), no protein binding, low MW — highly dialyzable. TCA, digoxin not dialyzable due to large Vd + protein binding."

11. Disposition

Tintinalli p.1193
  • Discharge: resolved acute toxicity + no end-organ damage + reliable follow-up + psychiatric clearance for intentional ingestions.
  • Observation (4–6 h): minor ingestions; await peak/decline of toxicant levels.
  • Admit floor / telemetry: ongoing antidote infusions, mild–moderate toxicity, sustained-release ingestions.
  • ICU: AMS, hemodynamic instability, respiratory failure, requiring HD/ECMO/HDI, severe acid-base derangements, intubation.
  • Psychiatric consultation for all intentional ingestions before discharge.
  • Poison control follow-up; discharge planning may include addiction services, social work for occupational/environmental exposures.

⚕️ ATLS 11th — Toxicology in Trauma

ATLS
  • ~30% of trauma victims have positive toxicology — alcohol most common.
  • Toxicology + trauma can mask each other (e.g., AMS attributed to ETOH when it's a head injury, or vice versa).
  • Always obtain alcohol level, drug screen, and APAP/salicylate level in trauma + AMS.
  • Empiric "coma cocktail" (glucose, naloxone, thiamine) appropriate in undifferentiated AMS.
  • RSI considerations: ketamine acceptable in undifferentiated; etomidate hemodynamically neutral; rocuronium for paralysis (avoid succ if hyperK from rhabdo).
  • Toxin-induced shock can mimic hemorrhagic shock — fluid resuscitation + antidote + tox panel.
Rosen source: Rosen is used to cross-check poisoned-patient resuscitation priorities, decontamination indications, antidote sequencing, and disposition pitfalls. Rosen vs Tintinalli: Tintinalli supplies core tables and chapter flow; Rosen adds bedside toxicology framing and resuscitation nuance.

📗 Rosen's EM 10th — Approach to the Poisoned Patient

Rosen's Ch.139
  • Same overall framework — ABCs + identify toxidrome + decontamination + antidote + supportive.
  • Rosen's emphasizes: "treat the patient, not the poison" — supportive care + monitoring is the most important intervention.
  • Activated charcoal: Rosen's lists single-dose AC as appropriate within 1 h, up to 4 h for sustained-release or anticholinergic ingestions (delayed gastric emptying).
  • Multi-dose AC: "CDPST" — Carbamazepine, Dapsone, Phenobarbital, Salicylate (debated), Theophylline.
  • HD criteria: EXTRIP recommendations published per drug — consult poison control for individual cases.
  • Pediatric considerations: different dose thresholds for many drugs; many "one pill can kill" agents (CCB, β-blocker, opioid, sulfonylurea, TCA, antimalarials).
  • Rosen's stresses: early consultation with regional poison control center (1-800-222-1222 in US); they have access to most current treatment recommendations.

Correct option. Read the full rationale below.
C. Diaphoresis + agitation + HTN
Incorrect option. Compare against the correct choice and rationale below.
D. Rigidity + hyperreflexia
Incorrect option. Compare against the correct choice and rationale below.
Answer: B. Classic opioid triad. Reference: Tintinalli Table 176-4.
End MCQ 4. Which feature distinguishes anticholinergic from sympathomimetic toxidrome?
A. Mydriasis
Incorrect option. Compare against the correct choice and rationale below.
B. Tachycardia
Incorrect option. Compare against the correct choice and rationale below.
C. Skin moisture: dry (anticholinergic) vs wet/diaphoretic (sympathomimetic)
Correct option. Read the full rationale below.
D. Hyperthermia
Incorrect option. Compare against the correct choice and rationale below.
Answer: C. Both cause mydriasis, tachycardia, HTN, hyperthermia. Skin distinguishes them.
End MCQ 5. The PHAILS mnemonic for substances NOT bound by activated charcoal includes all EXCEPT:
A. Pesticides
Incorrect option. Compare against the correct choice and rationale below.
B. Iron
Incorrect option. Compare against the correct choice and rationale below.
C. Acetaminophen
Correct option. Read the full rationale below.
D. Lithium
Incorrect option. Compare against the correct choice and rationale below.
Answer: C. PHAILS = Pesticides, Hydrocarbons, Acids/Alkali, Iron, Lithium, Solvents/Salts. APAP IS bound by AC.
End MCQ 6. First-line antidote for cyanide poisoning in fire smoke inhalation is:
A. Sodium nitrite alone
Incorrect option. Compare against the correct choice and rationale below.
B. Hydroxocobalamin (Cyanokit) 5 g IV
Correct option. Read the full rationale below.
C. Methylene blue
Incorrect option. Compare against the correct choice and rationale below.
D. Atropine
Incorrect option. Compare against the correct choice and rationale below.
Answer: B. Hydroxocobalamin preferred — doesn't worsen methemoglobinemia of CO co-poisoning.
End MCQ 7. Which drug is the antidote for β-blocker toxicity?
A. Atropine alone
Incorrect option. Compare against the correct choice and rationale below.
B. Glucagon (5 mg IV bolus → infusion)
Correct option. Read the full rationale below.
C. Calcium chloride alone
Incorrect option. Compare against the correct choice and rationale below.
D. Sodium bicarbonate
Incorrect option. Compare against the correct choice and rationale below.
Answer: B. Glucagon bypasses β-receptors via direct cAMP activation. High-dose insulin also useful.
End MCQ 8. Which drug is BEST removed by hemodialysis?
A. Tricyclic antidepressant
Incorrect option. Compare against the correct choice and rationale below.
B. Digoxin
Incorrect option. Compare against the correct choice and rationale below.
C. Lithium (low Vd, no protein binding)
Correct option. Read the full rationale below.
D. Iron
Incorrect option. Compare against the correct choice and rationale below.
Answer: C. Lithium is small Vd (~0.7), no protein binding, low MW — highly dialyzable.
End MCQ 9. Multidose activated charcoal is indicated for:
A. Iron OD
Incorrect option. Compare against the correct choice and rationale below.
B. Carbamazepine, Dapsone, Phenobarbital, Theophylline (CDPST)
Correct option. Read the full rationale below.
C. Salicylate alone (controversial)
Incorrect option. Compare against the correct choice and rationale below.
D. Acetaminophen
Incorrect option. Compare against the correct choice and rationale below.
Answer: B. CDPST mnemonic for drugs with enterohepatic circulation that benefit from multidose AC.
End MCQ 10. The classic finding distinguishing serotonin syndrome from NMS is:
A. Hyperthermia
Incorrect option. Compare against the correct choice and rationale below.
B. Lower extremity clonus + hyperreflexia (serotonin) vs lead-pipe rigidity (NMS)
Correct option. Read the full rationale below.
C. Altered mental status
Incorrect option. Compare against the correct choice and rationale below.
D. Autonomic instability
Incorrect option. Compare against the correct choice and rationale below.
Answer: B. Both share AMS + hyperthermia + autonomic instability. Clonus + hyperreflexia = serotonin; lead-pipe rigidity = NMS.
End MCQ 11. Pyridoxine is the antidote for which poisoning that causes refractory seizures?
A. Cocaine
Incorrect option. Compare against the correct choice and rationale below.
B. Isoniazid (INH)
Correct option. Read the full rationale below.
C. Methanol
Incorrect option. Compare against the correct choice and rationale below.
D. Acetaminophen
Incorrect option. Compare against the correct choice and rationale below.
Answer: B. INH depletes pyridoxine → GABA deficiency → refractory seizures. Pyridoxine 1 g per gram INH (or 5 g empiric).
End MCQ 12. A patient on quetiapine has urine drug screen 'positive' for amphetamines and methadone. The most likely explanation is:
A. Patient took both drugs
Incorrect option. Compare against the correct choice and rationale below.
B. Cross-reactive false-positive from quetiapine on UDS
Correct option. Read the full rationale below.
C. Lab error
Incorrect option. Compare against the correct choice and rationale below.
D. Quetiapine is a banned substance
Incorrect option. Compare against the correct choice and rationale below.
Answer: B. Quetiapine and several antihistamines/dextromethorphan/diphenhydramine cause false-positives on UDS.
End MCQ 13. Which is the FIRST-line agent for toxin-induced agitation?
A. Haloperidol
Incorrect option. Compare against the correct choice and rationale below.
B. Benzodiazepines (lorazepam, diazepam)
Correct option. Read the full rationale below.
C. Physical restraints alone
Incorrect option. Compare against the correct choice and rationale below.
D. Diphenhydramine
Incorrect option. Compare against the correct choice and rationale below.
Answer: B. Benzo first-line. Antipsychotics second (QT, dystonia, seizure risk).
End MCQ 14. Octreotide is the antidote for hypoglycemia from:
A. Insulin overdose
Incorrect option. Compare against the correct choice and rationale below.
B. Sulfonylurea overdose
Correct option. Read the full rationale below.
C. β-blocker
Incorrect option. Compare against the correct choice and rationale below.
D. Salicylate
Incorrect option. Compare against the correct choice and rationale below.
Answer: B. Sulfonylureas cause refractory hypoglycemia by stimulating insulin release; octreotide suppresses insulin secretion.
End MCQ 15. Fomepizole is the preferred antidote for:
A. Acetaminophen
Incorrect option. Compare against the correct choice and rationale below.
B. Methanol or ethylene glycol
Correct option. Read the full rationale below.
C. Salicylate
Incorrect option. Compare against the correct choice and rationale below.
D. Carbon monoxide
Incorrect option. Compare against the correct choice and rationale below.
Answer: B. Fomepizole inhibits alcohol dehydrogenase — blocks formation of toxic metabolites.
End MCQ 16. The 'I STUMBLED' mnemonic describes drugs that:
A. Cause coma
Incorrect option. Compare against the correct choice and rationale below.
B. Are removed by hemodialysis
Correct option. Read the full rationale below.
C. Cause seizures
Incorrect option. Compare against the correct choice and rationale below.
D. Cause hyperthermia
Incorrect option. Compare against the correct choice and rationale below.
Answer: B. Isopropanol, Salicylate, Theophylline, Uremia, Methanol/Methotrexate, Barbiturate, Lithium, Ethylene glycol, Dabigatran — dialyzable.
End MCQ 17. Which is INAPPROPRIATE for a patient with acute hydrocarbon ingestion?
A. ABCs / supportive care
Incorrect option. Compare against the correct choice and rationale below.
B. Activated charcoal (provides no benefit and ↑ aspiration risk)
Correct option. Read the full rationale below.
C. CXR for aspiration
Incorrect option. Compare against the correct choice and rationale below.
D. Observation
Incorrect option. Compare against the correct choice and rationale below.
Answer: B. AC doesn't bind hydrocarbons + induces vomiting → aspiration. Reference: PHAILS / Tintinalli p.1192.
End MCQ 18. The cholinergic mnemonic 'DUMBBELS' includes:
A. Dilated pupils
Incorrect option. Compare against the correct choice and rationale below.
B. Defecation, Urination, Miosis, Bradycardia/Bronchorrhea/Bronchospasm, Emesis, Lacrimation, Salivation
Correct option. Read the full rationale below.
C. Dry skin, Mydriasis, Bradycardia
Incorrect option. Compare against the correct choice and rationale below.
D. Diaphoresis, Mydriasis, Bradycardia
Incorrect option. Compare against the correct choice and rationale below.
Answer: B. DUMBBELS — cholinergic (organophosphate). Note miosis (NOT mydriasis); bradycardia (NOT tachycardia).
End MCQ 19. A patient with mixed ETOH + benzodiazepine OD with respiratory depression. Best management:
A. Flumazenil 0.2 mg IV (reverses benzo)
Incorrect option. Compare against the correct choice and rationale below.
B. Supportive care (intubation if needed); avoid flumazenil in mixed OD
Correct option. Read the full rationale below.
C. Naloxone
Incorrect option. Compare against the correct choice and rationale below.
D. Activated charcoal alone
Incorrect option. Compare against the correct choice and rationale below.
Answer: B. Flumazenil contraindicated in mixed/unknown OD (precipitates seizures, especially with TCA). Supportive care + intubation.
End MCQ 20. Which 'one pill can kill' agent is a major pediatric concern?
A. Acetaminophen
Incorrect option. Compare against the correct choice and rationale below.
B. CCB, β-blocker, opioid, sulfonylurea, TCA, antimalarials
Correct option. Read the full rationale below.
C. Multivitamins
Incorrect option. Compare against the correct choice and rationale below.
D. Penicillin
Incorrect option. Compare against the correct choice and rationale below.
Answer: B. Single dose of these classes can be lethal in toddlers — extended observation + admit. Reference: Rosen's pediatric tox.

🔑 Key Points (High-Yield)

  1. "Treat the patient, not the poison" — supportive care + monitoring saves more lives than antidotes.
  2. Coma cocktail: glucose + naloxone + thiamine. Avoid flumazenil in mixed OD.
  3. Anticholinergic vs Sympathomimetic — distinguish by SKIN: dry hot vs diaphoretic.
  4. Cholinergic mnemonics: SLUDGE-M (S/L/U/D/G/E + Miosis) and DUMBBELS.
  5. Opioid triad: miosis + CNS depression + respiratory depression.
  6. Serotonin vs NMS: clonus + hyperreflexia (serotonin, lower > upper) vs lead-pipe rigidity (NMS).
  7. PHAILS — substances NOT bound by activated charcoal: Pesticides, Hydrocarbons, Acids/Alkali, Iron, Lithium, Solvents/Salts.
  8. Multi-dose AC indications (CDPST): Carbamazepine, Dapsone, Phenobarbital, Salicylate (debated), Theophylline.
  9. Whole-bowel irrigation for: iron, lithium, lead, sustained-release, body packers/stuffers.
  10. Urinary alkalinization indications: salicylate, phenobarbital, chlorophenoxy. Need K⁺ replacement.
  11. "I STUMBLED" dialyzable drugs: Isopropanol, Salicylate, Theophylline, Uremia, Methanol/Methotrexate, Barbiturate, Lithium, Ethylene glycol, Dabigatran.
  12. Cyanide: Hydroxocobalamin preferred for smoke inhalation.
  13. β-blocker / CCB: Calcium + glucagon + high-dose insulin (HDI).
  14. TCA / cocaine wide-QRS: Sodium bicarbonate.
  15. Lipid emulsion (Intralipid 20%) for local anesthetic + lipophilic cardiotoxin.
  16. Standard urine drug screens have BIG false-positive AND false-negative rates — clinical correlation essential.
  17. Avoid flumazenil in mixed OD; avoid phenytoin for toxin-induced seizures (Class IB Na block).
  18. Antipyretics ineffective for toxin-induced hyperthermia — cool actively + sedate.
  19. Poison Control Center 1-800-222-1222 (US) — call early.
  20. "One pill can kill" pediatric: CCB, β-blocker, opioid, sulfonylurea, TCA, antimalarials, methadone, camphor.
